title: Johnson transformation of non normal data to normal
label2: Select a non-normal variable to be transformed to normal using the best fitting Johnson family (SB, SL, or SU)
variableSelcted: A non-normal variable to be transformed
johnsonColName: (Optional) Specify a new variable name to store the transformed values. Otherwise <variable_jtrans> will be created
pvalueCriterion: P-Value criterion to select the transformation - the best transformation must have an Anderson-Darling normality p-value above this criterion (default is 0.10)
forceTransformChk: Force the transformation i.e. transform and store the values even if the original data already pass the normality test or if the best fit does not meet the p-value criterion above
digits: Digits - rounds to the specified number of decimal places

help.title: Johnson transformation of non-normal data to normal
help.body:
Description
Transforms a non-normal variable to normal by selecting the optimal function from the three Johnson families of distributions - SB, SL, and SU - where B, L, and U refer to the variable being bounded, lognormal, and unbounded respectively

This dialog implements the algorithm (Chou, Polansky and Mason, 1998, with the parameter estimation formulas of Slifker and Shapiro, 1980). The implementation is self-contained in R - it does not depend on the archived 'jtrans' package. Only the 'nortest' package is required

1. A grid of Z values from 0.25 to 1.25 with an increment of 0.01 is considered
2. For each Z, sample quantiles x1, x2, x3, x4 are computed at the standard normal percentiles -3Z, -Z, Z, 3Z (interpolated order statistics, R quantile type 5, i.e. rank = n*p + 0.5) and the spreads m = x4 - x3, n = x2 - x1, p = x3 - x2 give the quantile ratio QR = mn/p²
3. QR > 1 selects the SU family, QR < 1 the SB family, and QR approximately 1 the SL family. The family parameters Gamma (γ), Eta (η), Epsilon (ε), Lambda (λ) are estimated from the four quantiles. Fits with invalid parameters (e.g. SB bounds not containing the data) are skipped
4. The transformed data for each Z is tested for normality with the Anderson-Darling (AD) test
5. The transformation with the largest AD p-value that is greater than the p-value criterion (default 0.10) is selected as the best transformation

Unlike Box-Cox, the Johnson transformation can be used with negative values and zeros

Output
- Sample size table (Total, N non-missing, N* missing)
- Normal probability plot with AD statistic and p-value for the original data
- "Select a Transformation" plot of the AD p-value against each Z value, with a horizontal reference line at the p-value criterion (Ref P) and a vertical reference line at the best Z
- Best transformation type (SB, SL, or SU), Z for best fit, P-value for best fit, the estimated parameters Gamma (γ), Eta (η), Epsilon (ε), Lambda (λ), and the Johnson transformation function
- Normal probability plot with AD statistic and p-value for the transformed data
- A new variable containing the transformed values. The transformation type and parameter estimates are stored as attributes (jtrans_type, jtrans_z, jtrans_gamma, jtrans_eta, jtrans_epsilon, jtrans_lambda) of the new variable so the transformation is traceable and an inverse transformation remains possible

The three Johnson transformation functions
SB (bounded): γ + η * Ln( (X - ε) / (λ + ε - X) )
SL (lognormal): γ + η * Ln( X - ε )
SU (unbounded): γ + η * Asinh( (X - ε) / λ )

If the original data already follow a normal distribution (AD p-value at or above the criterion), or if no candidate transformation meets the p-value criterion, no transformed variable is stored - unless the "Force the transformation" option is checked

A minimum of 8 non-missing observations is required (limit of the Anderson-Darling test); at least 20 for a reliable transformation

References: Chou, Y.M., Polansky, A.M., Mason, R.L. (1998) "Transforming Non-Normal Data to Normality in Statistical Process Control", Journal of Quality Technology, 30(2); Slifker, J.F., Shapiro, S.S. (1980) "The Johnson System: Selection and Parameter Estimation", Technometrics, 22(2)
